en: Just as a plantain tree, when split apart along with all its constituent parts,
is found to be nothing at all, so too is a person when split apart along with the elements.
Therefore, the Victors have declared that "all phenomena are without self."
And by them, the entire sixfold set of elements has been determined, yet that is not [found] in reality.
Thus, neither a self nor a non-self is found according to the way things truly are;
therefore, the Great Sage has warded off the views concerning self and non-self.
"Whatever has been seen, heard, and so forth, the Sage has declared to be neither true nor false;
for from a position there arises its opposite, and both of these do not exist in reality.
Thus, from the perspective of ultimate truth, this world transcends both truth and falsehood.
And for this very reason, in reality, one does not approach [the view] that "it exists" or "it does not exist.
How could an omniscient one speak of that which is thus in no way [existent],
as being finite or infinite, dual or non-dual?
Countless Buddhas have passed away, as many will come, and there are those in the present;

the end of sentient beings is considered to be produced from them throughout the three times. There is no cause for the increase of the world, nor is there any decrease possible within the three times.
How could the Omniscient One have left its prior limit undeclared?
This is indeed the profundity of the Dharma: that which is secret from ordinary people—the fact that the world is like an illusion—is the nectar of the Buddhas' teaching.
Just as the birth and the end of an illusory elephant are perceived,
yet neither its birth nor its end exists in reality;
so too, for the world which is like an illusion, there is only birth and end.
In ultimate reality, neither birth nor end is perceived.
Just as an illusory elephant comes from nowhere and goes nowhere,
it does not abide as a real entity because it is merely a delusion of the mind.
Likewise, the world is like an illusion; it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
Because it is merely a delusion of the mind, it does not abide as a real entity.
Thus, what is this world in reality, its nature transcending the three times?

Whether it exists, does not exist, or even might exist—apart from conventional usage—it is for this fourfold reason, and no other, that the Buddha left [the questions] undeclared: whether the world is finite, infinite, both, or neither. (RATNA_02.14–15)
If even the gross impurity of the body— which is within the range of direct perception and is constantly being observed— does not remain in the mind,
then how much less so this True Dharma, which is extremely subtle, profound, and free from any substratum?
How could that which is not directly perceived enter the mind with ease?
Having awakened, the Sage became inclined toward Nirvana rather than teaching the Dharma,
realizing that this Dharma is difficult for people to understand due to its extreme profundity.
This Dharma, when wrongly understood, destroys the unwise,
for he sinks into the impurity of the view of non-existence. Furthermore, from this wrong understanding, another fool becomes conceited, imagining himself to be a scholar.
One whose self is ruined by rejection goes headfirst to the Avīci hell.
Just as one meets with destruction through food that is poorly consumed, so too,
through food well consumed, one enjoys long life, health, strength, and happiness.
Thus, through a wrong understanding of this, one meets with destruction;
but through a correct understanding of it, one attains happiness and unsurpassed awakening.
Therefore, having abandoned both rejection and the nihilistic view regarding this, [one should proceed].
Exert yourself toward right knowledge for the sake of accomplishing all goals.
Because of a lack of full understanding of this Dharma, ego-grasping persists;
from that arises wholesome and unwholesome karma, and from that, wholesome and unwholesome birth.
Therefore, as long as the Dharma that destroys the ego is not understood,
remain devoted to the practices of generosity, ethical discipline, and patience. O King,
let all actions have the Dharma as their beginning and the Dharma as their middle.
One who accomplishes those things rooted in Dharma does not suffer, neither in this world nor in the next.
From Dharma comes fame and happiness; there is no fear here for one about to die, and there is abundant happiness in the next world. Therefore, always devote yourself to Dharma.
Dharma alone is the supreme policy; by dharma the world is won over.
For when the world is won over, one is not deceived either in this world or in the next. But by a policy that is contrary to dharma, the world is alienated.
Because they cause displeasure to the world, they find no joy neither in this life nor in the next. Devoted to deceiving others, this is a miserable path leading to the lower realms;
how have the ignorant made this science of misfortune into a science of profit?
How can one who is intent on deceiving others and possesses [only] worldly policy be successful in his purpose,
by which he deceives only himself for many thousands of births?
Seeking what is unpleasant for the enemy, abandon faults and take recourse in virtues.
Indeed, the attainment of one's own welfare would itself be unpleasant to an enemy.
Through generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and consistency between words and deeds—
by these means, win over the world and likewise gather the Dharma.
Just as truth produces a firm confidence in kings,
so too does even that which is untrue produce extreme mistrust in them.
Truth that is not consistent with fact is not truly elevated in its essential meaning.
Truth is that which is exclusively beneficial, while the other is falsehood because it is harmful.
Just as a brilliant act of generosity on the part of kings conceals their faults,
so too does their miserliness destroy the entirety of their virtues.
For one who is tranquil there is depth; from depth comes supreme dignity;
from dignity comes radiance and authoritative command; therefore, devote yourself to tranquility.
Through wisdom, one's intellect becomes unshakeable, independent of others, and steadfast.
The king is not outwitted; therefore, be devoted to wisdom.
A lord of men who possesses the four excellences—truth, generosity, tranquility, and wisdom—is praised by gods and humans alike, just like the Dharma itself which possesses the four excellences.
For one who constantly sits together with those who speak with restraint, who are pure, and who are stainless through wisdom and compassion, wisdom and the Dharma increase.
Those who speak what is beneficial are rare; those who listen are even rarer still.
Among them, those who act swiftly upon what is beneficial are the most difficult to find. Therefore, knowing that what is beneficial may be unpleasant, practice it immediately;
just as a self-possessed person would drink even a bitter medicine for the sake of health.
Always contemplate the impermanence of life, health, and sovereignty; then, filled with a sense of spiritual urgency, you will apply yourself to the Dharma with single-minded devotion.
Seeing that death is inevitable, and that suffering arises from evil deeds as well as after one has died, [you will turn away from them].
You ought not to commit evil even for the sake of happiness in this life.
If fearlessness is seen in one moment and fear is seen in another moment,
if you find consolation in the one, why do you not feel fear in the other?
From intoxicants comes humiliation in the world, the neglect of one’s duties, and the loss of wealth;
through delusion, one commits improper acts— therefore, always renounce intoxicants.
